content: Public health laboratories play a critical role in overseeing quality control, coordinating proficiency testing, and providing training and certification for personnel. When hand-held devices are used to conduct blood lead analysis outside traditional laboratory settings, robust information systems must be established. These systems should ensure that blood test results are systematically reported to the appropriate public health agencies. This is essential to incorporate valuable screening data into state tracking systems. Ideally, new blood lead testing devices designed for field or office use should have the capability to automatically collect and report blood lead test results. The Health Care Financing Administration (HCFA) mandates blood lead screening for all young children enrolled in Medicaid, with no current allowance for deviation from this requirement. However, HCFA is collaborating with the Advisory Committee on Childhood Lead Poisoning Prevention (ACCLPP) to develop a targeted screening approach for Medicaid-enrolled children in states where sufficient data supports such a policy. ACCLPP, in partnership with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), has agreed to assist HCFA by developing scientifically based criteria for targeted screening. Data indicates that a significant proportion of children aged 1–5 years enrolled in Medicaid have elevated blood lead levels (BLLs) of ≥10 µg/dL. Among children in this age group with BLLs ≥20 µg/dL, 83% are enrolled in Medicaid. Despite legal requirements, most young children in Medicaid have not undergone blood lead screening. Consequently, an estimated 352,000 children with elevated BLLs remain unidentified and untreated. Failure to comply with Medicaid blood lead screening requirements results in missed opportunities to efficiently identify children with elevated BLLs who could benefit from medical and public health follow-up services. To address this, health-care providers and health plans should ensure that blood lead screening, diagnostic, and treatment services are provided to Medicaid-enrolled children. Additionally, children with elevated BLLs should be referred for environmental and public health follow-up services. States must also ensure that young children enrolled in Medicaid receive the appropriate blood lead screening and follow-up care to which they are legally entitled. The Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (MMWR) series is prepared by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). It is available free of charge in electronic format and can also be accessed in paper format through a paid subscription.
